tasks.commitBody: Every hard-capped list read in the app now answers the question the silent prefix never did: is this everything? The rule is per read and there are only two honest answers — a bound that provably cannot be reached, said in a comment naming why, in the one comment shape the codebase already had for it; or a surface that tells the user the list is partial. The detection costs nothing new on the wire: Entu list responses have carried the true total all along in a count field the display readers were typing away, and two live probes settled what the documentation never said — the count is the caller-visible total at every rights tier, a row the caller cannot see appearing in neither the count nor the page, so a notice may show real numbers without leaking anything, and a collection sitting exactly at its cap is distinguishable from a truncated one only by that count, which is why comparing lengths against limits is forbidden in this diff. The notices are one shared shape, visible and persistent for as long as the condition holds, in all four languages. The cascade delete guards that already refused to act on a partial list stay byte-identical — they were the third shape, found correct. The season panel's written admission that its list under-reports is narrowed to what is still true now that the list can tell. Two guards outlive the sweep: a source-scan spec asserts every list read states its limit explicitly, because the vendor's omitted-limit default of one hundred is a cap tighter than any we ever wrote and invisible in both directions; and the count dependency is written down where it is used, citing the two probe ledgers, because a privacy-relevant guarantee resting on undocumented behaviour is a fact to be findable, not absorbed. Paging, which the vendor documents as one parameter, stays available where a list is genuinely long — the preference for a notice is about the reader, not the wire. STATED CHOICES: <GREEN agent fills>.
